examShortTricks: Trick 1: Six-step classical protocol: collection of variability → evaluation and selection of parents → cross-hybridisation → selection of superior recombinants → testing/release (multi-year field trials) — the ordered list IS the answer.
Trick 2: Examples: semi-dwarf wheat (Norman Borlaug, Sonalika/Kalyan Sona), rice (Jaya, IR-8), sugarcane (Saccharum × Saccharum barbari), millets hybrid — quote two.
Trick 3: Fortification breeding: Atlas 66 wheat (high protein) and iron-fortified spinach varieties — the nutrition angle.
Trick 4: Mutation breeding: gamma rays/chemicals create variation (mohan rice variety); polyploidy via colchicine — the non-conventional methods.
keyPoints: Plant breeding combines desirable traits from different plants into high-yield varieties.
Steps: germplasm collection, hybridisation, selection, testing, release.
Semi-dwarf wheat and rice varieties powered the Green Revolution.
Mutation breeding and polyploidy create additional variability.
practiceQuestions: Q. List the main steps of classical plant breeding. (3 marks) — as above in order.
Q. Name two high-yielding semi-dwarf wheat varieties of India. (1 mark) — Sonalika, Kalyan Sona.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Definition: protein from MICROBIAL biomass (Spirulina, Methylophilus methylotrophus, yeast, Chlorella) grown on waste — the microbe names are the marks.
Trick 2: Merits: high protein (Spirulina >50%), fast growth (microbes double in hours), uses waste substrate, little land/water — four merits.
Trick 3: 250 kg cow vs 250 g microbe comparison: microbe produces ~25 tonnes protein/day vs cow 200 g — the classic numerical contrast.
Trick 4: Limitation: public acceptance, texture/taste, contamination control — one line for the balanced answer.
keyPoints: SCP is edible protein from microbial cultures.
Spirulina and Methylophilus are standard SCP organisms.
Microbial growth is far faster than livestock protein production.
SCP uses industrial/agricultural waste as substrate.
practiceQuestions: Q. What is SCP? Give one example organism. (2 marks) — single-cell protein; Spirulina.
Q. Give two advantages of SCP. (1 mark) — rapid production, low land requirement.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Branches in one line each: dairy (milk), poultry (eggs/meat), apiculture (bees/honey), pisciculture (fish), sericulture (silk) — five branches with products.
Trick 2: Cattle breeds: exotic high-yield (Jersey, Holstein-Friesian) vs indigenous hardy (Sahiwal, Gir, Red Sindhi); cross-breeding combines both — the two-column answer.
Trick 3: Poultry breeds: layers vs broilers; improved breeds need feed, hygiene, vaccination — management triad.
Trick 4: Bee-keeping: Apis indica common; Italian bee A. mellifera high honey yield; apiary location near flowers — the apiculture specifics.
keyPoints: Animal husbandry covers cattle, poultry, fish, bees and silkworm management.
Cross-breeding indigenous hardiness with exotic yield improves breeds.
Poultry needs balanced feed, sanitation and vaccination.
Apiculture yields honey and wax; Italian bees are high producers.
practiceQuestions: Q. Name two indigenous and two exotic cattle breeds. (1 mark) — Sahiwal/Gir; Jersey/Holstein.
Q. What is sericulture? (1 mark) — rearing silkworms for silk production.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Biofertilizer bank: Rhizobium (legume nodules), Azotobacter/Azospirillum (free-living), blue-green algae Anabaena/Nostoc (rice fields), mycorrhiza (Glomus — P uptake, drought resistance) — four classes with roles.
Trick 2: Organic farming triad: organic manures/compost, biofertilizers, IPM (biocontrol) instead of chemicals — the sustainable package.
Trick 3: Merits: cheaper, renewable, no soil/water pollution, maintain soil fertility long-term — four merits for the 2-mark answer.
Trick 4: Cyanobacteria fix ~significant N in paddy — the rice-specific application.
keyPoints: Biofertilizers supply nutrients through living organisms.
Rhizobium symbiosis fixes nitrogen in legume root nodules.
Mycorrhizal fungi improve phosphorus and water uptake.
Sustainable agriculture minimises chemical inputs and preserves soil health.
practiceQuestions: Q. Name two biofertilizers and their roles. (2 marks) — Rhizobium (N-fixation in legumes); mycorrhiza (P uptake).
Q. Why are biofertilizers eco-friendly? (1 mark) — they replace chemical fertilisers that pollute soil and water.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Five products with microbes — curd (Lactobacillus, lactic acid), dough/idli-dosa (bacteria + yeast CO2), toddy (Saccharomyces), cheese (Propionibacterium holes; Roquefort fungi), bread (Saccharomyces cerevisiae).
Trick 2: 'Roquefort cheese ripened by blue-green fungi; big holes in Swiss cheese from CO2 of Propionibacterium' — the two cheese specifics.
Trick 3: LAB converts milk to curd by producing lactic acid which coagulates casein and also checks disease-causing microbes — the dual benefit line.
keyPoints: Lactobacillus converts milk to curd by lactic acid fermentation.
Yeast (Saccharomyces) leavens bread and ferments toddy.
Bacteria ferment dosa/idli batter.
Cheese ripening uses specific bacteria and fungi.
practiceQuestions: Q. Which microbe makes curd from milk and how? (2 marks) — Lactobacillus; lactic acid coagulates milk protein.
Q. What gives Swiss cheese its large holes? (1 mark) — CO2 released by Propionibacterium sharmanii.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Antibiotic: Penicillium notatum/chrysogenum → penicillin (Fleming 1928, Chain & Florey purified); 'antibiotic' = against life — the discovery story earns the mark.
Trick 2: Alcohol: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (brewer's yeast) ferments malted grains/fruit juice; distilled spirits vs beer/wine — the yeast is the same in all.
Trick 3: Citric acid: Aspergillus niger; also acetic acid (Acetobacter), lactic acid (Lactobacillus) — the industrial chemicals table.
Trick 4: Fermenters provide: sterile medium, aeration, temperature control, pH — the four conditions for industrial scale-up.
keyPoints: Penicillin is produced industrially by Penicillium.
Yeast fermentation produces ethanol for beverages.
Aspergillus niger yields citric acid commercially.
Large-scale microbial production happens in fermenters.
practiceQuestions: Q. Which organism produces penicillin? (1 mark) — Penicillium notatum/chrysogenum.
Q. Name the microbe used for industrial citric acid production. (1 mark) — Aspergillus niger.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Biocontrol bank: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt toxin kills insect larvae — Bt cotton carries the gene), Trichoderma (fungus vs plant pathogens), ladybird/Aphatelina beetles vs aphids, Baculovirus (insect-specific, harmless to plants/birds/fish).
Trick 2: Merit line: biocontrol is target-specific, no chemical residue, no resistance build-up — the eco advantage over pesticides.
Trick 3: Biofertilizers: Rhizobium, Azospirillum, cyanobacteria, mycorrhiza — reuse of the earlier list with the biocontrol contrast.
Trick 4: Bt toxin detail: inactive protoxin → activated in insect gut (alkaline pH) → binds midgut cells → lysis — the activation mechanism is the 2-marker.
keyPoints: Biocontrol uses natural enemies/microbes instead of chemical pesticides.
Bt toxin from Bacillus thuringiensis kills caterpillar pests.
Trichoderma controls fungal plant diseases.
Biofertilizers like Rhizobium enrich soil nitrogen naturally.
practiceQuestions: Q. How does Bt toxin kill insects? (2 marks) — inactive protoxin becomes active in the alkaline insect gut and punches holes in midgut cells.
Q. Give one example of microbial biocontrol of fungi. (1 mark) — Trichoderma against soil-borne pathogens.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Bioremediation: microbes degrade pollutants — Pseudomonas putida (oil spills, 'superbugs'), bacteria clean sewage in secondary treatment; the definition + example pair.
Trick 2: Biogas: anaerobic digestion — methanogens (Methanobacterium) in cow dung produce CH4 (~55–60%), CO2, H2S; gobar gas plant: mixing tank → digester → gas holder.
Trick 3: Methanogens are ANAEROBES — that is why the digester is sealed; cow dung inoculates the culture — the two conditions.
Trick 4: Uses of biogas: cooking, lighting; sludge residue = fertiliser — the dual product line.
keyPoints: Bioremediation uses microbes to remove pollutants.
Pseudomonas putida degrades hydrocarbons in oil spills.
Biogas is mainly methane produced by anaerobic methanogens.
Cow dung slurry is the standard inoculum for biogas plants.
practiceQuestions: Q. Which microbes produce biogas and under what condition? (2 marks) — methanogenic bacteria under anaerobic conditions.
Q. What is bioremediation? (1 mark) — use of microbes to degrade environmental pollutants.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Restriction enzymes: cut palindromic sites; EcoRI = E. coli restriction I; produce sticky ends (5' overhangs) — the nomenclature and sticky ends are the marks.
Trick 2: Vector requirements: origin of replication (ori), selectable marker (antibiotic resistance), cloning site (MCS), small size, high copy number — five criteria.
Trick 3: Competent host: CaCl2 + cold shock (0 °C → 42 °C) makes E. coli take up plasmids; alternatives: microinjection, gene gun (biolistics), electroporation — the methods list.
Trick 4: Insertional inactivation: insert in lacZ/blue-white screening — the selection trick worth a mark.
keyPoints: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific palindromic sequences.
Sticky ends allow recombinant DNA ligation.
Vectors need ori, selectable marker and multiple cloning sites.
Host cells are made competent by CaCl2 treatment or physical methods.
practiceQuestions: Q. What are sticky ends and why are they useful? (2 marks) — staggered single-stranded overhangs that pair with complementary ends for ligation.
Q. Name three features a cloning vector must have. (1 mark) — ori, selectable marker, MCS.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: DNA isolation: cell lysis (lysozyme/EDTA/detergent) → protease/RNase → chilled ethanol precipitation ('spooling') — the three-step order.
Trick 2: PCR three steps: denaturation 94–95 °C, primer annealing 50–60 °C, extension 72 °C (Taq polymerase) — temperatures ARE the marks; 30 cycles ≈ 10⁹ copies.
Trick 3: Gel electrophoresis: DNA moves to the anode (negative charge), smaller fragments faster; ethidium bromide + UV visualises; compare with a ladder.
Trick 4: Gene transfer: microinjection (direct into cell), gene gun (gold particles), disarmed Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium (plants) — three routes.
keyPoints: DNA is extracted by lysis, enzyme digestion and ethanol precipitation.
PCR amplifies DNA through denaturation, annealing and extension cycles.
Agarose gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size.
Genes enter cells via microinjection, biolistics or Agrobacterium vectors.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why is Taq polymerase used in PCR? (1 mark) — it is thermostable and survives the denaturation step.
Q. Toward which electrode does DNA migrate in gel electrophoresis? (1 mark) — the anode (+), as DNA is negatively charged.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Human insulin: two-chain A (21 aa) + B (30 aa) linked by disulphide; proinsulin → C-peptide removed; engineered in E. coli since 1983 — the chain numbers are the marks.
Trick 2: Gene therapy: ADA deficiency — lymphocytes from the patient, functional ADA gene inserted by retrovirus, cells returned (ex vivo); marrow transplant as alternative.
Trick 3: Other products: hGH, interferon, blood clotting factor VIII, vaccines (Hepatitis B surface antigen in yeast) — the product bank.
Trick 4: Molecular diagnosis: ELISA (antigen–antibody), PCR (pathogen/mutation detection) — the two diagnostic tools.
keyPoints: Humulin (human insulin) is made by engineered bacteria.
Insulin is synthesised as proinsulin; the C-peptide is removed to mature it.
Gene therapy replaces a defective gene (e.g. ADA deficiency).
ELISA and PCR are standard molecular diagnostic methods.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why is recombinant insulin better than extracted pancreas insulin? (1 mark) — unlimited supply, identical to human insulin, no allergic reactions.
Q. Name the first disease treated by gene therapy. (1 mark) — ADA (adenosine deaminase) deficiency.
